𝗥𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘂𝗲 𝗦𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗚𝗿𝗼𝘄 𝗙𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗧𝗵𝗮𝗻 𝗛𝗲𝗮𝗱𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁 
For decades, SIs have made money on SAP programs in two ways. 

The pyramid. Sell senior people, then gradually replace them with juniors at nearly the same rate. 
The tail. Accept a thin margin through go-live, then make it back in AMS, where the cost structure is lighter and the contract runs for years. 

Both depend on selling scope and billing hours. Parts of the traditional scope are shrinking. The hours are the SIs to redesign. 

──────────────── 
𝗟𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗦𝗰𝗼𝗽𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝗦𝗲𝗹𝗹 
Clean core cuts custom development and enhancements. 

On fixed-fee programs, that was also where margin often came back: every change request billed separately, frequently at a better rate. 
Clients have bought into the argument. They expect fit-to-standard and question every change request. 
SAP is embedding more AI into the product and taking a larger role in onboarding, transformation preparation, and methodology services around RISE. Work the SI once owned is moving to SAP, becoming automated, or disappearing. 

Much of that is outside the SIs control. 

──────────────── 
𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝗜 𝗪𝗶𝗻𝘀 𝗜𝘁 𝗕𝗮𝗰𝗸 
What the SI does control is how many hours a program takes. 
The biggest near-term gains from AI helpers are often not in configuration or code, but in everything around the system: testing first, then status reports, meeting notes, documentation, training material, cutover checklists, data validation, and after go-live, ticket triage. 

──────────────── 
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗽 
AI does not give back people. It gives back fragments. 
Two hours of a PMs day. A third of a testers week. Fragments do not staff another program. 

So on a fixed fee, program margin goes up, utilization goes down, and EBITDA does not move. 
The cost of those hours is still paid. Nobody bills them. EBITDA moves only when margin and utilization move together. 

──────────────── 
𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗠𝗮𝗸𝗲𝘀 𝗜𝘁 𝗪𝗼𝗿𝗸 
Fixed fee first. Under time and materials, every hour saved is revenue handed to the client. T&M makes sense only as a deliberate choice: a strategic account, a new capability, a reference. 

Then pool the work AI touches. Testing, PMO, documentation, and first-line support run as shared services across programs, not embedded in each one. Fragments from five programs add up to people who can be redeployed. 

Then a hiring plan that assumes AI. When there is no new work, the saving becomes real only through the next hires that are never made. 

The firms that design for all three will show revenue growing faster than headcount. The rest will report better program margins and wonder why EBITDA never followed.

Cutting entry-level hiring saves money this year and leaves an expertise gap in about ten.

That was the argument at a closed-door Digiday event last week, where an agency owner said they've stopped recruiting college graduates because AI handles junior tasks.

→ The hiring freeze. The counterargument in the room was that today's senior staff will retire, and the people who would have replaced them won't have learned the work. The proposed fixes were concrete: redesign junior roles rather than eliminate them, pair experienced staff with younger colleagues, and fund formal AI training with livable wages for interns. For anyone who leads a team, the practical step is to list the five judgment calls you make in a normal week that a first-year person once learned by doing, then assign each one an owner.

→ Sephora and TikTok Shop. Sephora put about 2,300 products on TikTok Shop and launched a $265 set, valued at $327, available only there, with creator Mikayla Nogueira, a co-founder of POV Beauty, hosting the launch livestream. Digiday reports TikTok Shop is now the fourth-largest U.S. health and beauty retailer. The mechanics matter more than the platform: an exclusive SKU with a creator is a different contract than a sponsored post, and the metric to watch is second-purchase rate, since analysts warn that heavy couponing can undercut a premium brand.

Two more in today's video: → Hoka is targeting the marathon training period before the November 2 race, not race day, and its Q1 sales and admin spend rose 13% against 8% revenue growth, so measure the run-up before you copy it. → Subway's revenue fell 6% in 2025 and it closed 729 locations; its U.S. CMO says losing existing customers while gaining new ones doesn't add up, so count your twelve-month losses against wins.

If you lead a team, what's your plan for who learns the work that entry-level jobs used to teach?

Small businesses are heading into Q4 more optimistic . . . and apparently spending more money on AI.

Citizens’ new Business Pulse, released this morning, found improving sentiment among small and midsize businesses, steady hiring plans and increased AI investment.

I wonder how many companies actually know what that AI spend looks like across the business. Twenty bucks a month for an employee to draft emails is one thing. An AI tool connected to customer data, company files, contracts or financial information is something else entirely.

And those purchases dont always arrive through the IT department anymore. An employee finds a tool, enters a credit card, connects an account and gets to work.

At some point, the AI budget becomes an internal-controls issue.

Not because AI is uniquely dangerous. Because businesses should probably know which outside systems have access to their information and what theyre allowed to do with it.

I suspect plenty of companies are going to discover they have a much larger AI stack than anyone intentionally approved.

Commercial HVAC Service Sales is undergoing a major shift. Here’s what’s driving the market right now.

The traditional "break-fix" and basic "filter-and-belt" maintenance sales model is officially losing ground. Three major developments are reshaping what commercial facility directors expect from their service partners:

1️⃣ The Rise of "HVAC-as-a-Service" (HaaS): Facility managers facing tight capital budgets are moving away from traditional CapEx purchases. Instead, they're signing multi-year service contracts where monitoring, continuous optimization, automated maintenance, and equipment performance are bundled into a predictable monthly OpEx fee. Reps who know how to sell financial outcomes instead of just mechanical agreements are winning big.

2️⃣ Predictive AI Diagnostics as a Closing Tool: Building Automation Systems (BAS) and cloud-connected sensors now flag micro-inefficiencies and refrigerant leaks long before a chiller or VRF unit fails. Top commercial sales reps are leveraging live building data during sales pitches to demonstrate guaranteed energy savings and reduced operational risk upfront.

3️⃣ The 2026 Commercial VRF Low-GWP Shift: With regulatory phase-outs hitting commercial Variable Refrigerant Flow (VRF) equipment and moving the market toward low-GWP refrigerants (like R-32 and R-454B), building owners are looking for long-term guidance. Sales engineering teams that proactively build 5-year compliance and service roadmaps for clients are capturing dominant market share.

The takeaway for hiring managers:

The profile of a successful Commercial Service Sales Rep has evolved. The reps commanding top-tier compensation packages right now aren't just relationship-builders, they are tech-literate, consultative advisors who understand building analytics, energy ROI, and modern contract structuring.

Quote: "Molly Liu and Aman Puri are tackling the U.S. accounting shortage from another angle — a global one. On Monday, they announced that their AI-powered talent marketplace MAVI, founded in 2023, has officially emerged from stealth. The service helps connect U.S. companies with top AI-proficient global financial and accounting talent within days.Speaking to TechCrunch, Liu, the company’s co-CEO, pointed out the problems facing the U.S. accounting industry today — mainly that the profession is shrinking and even those left aren’t necessarily fluent in the AI skills needed to help their enterprises grow. At the same time, she said, many U.S. companies don’t like the idea of working with global talent, either because it’s complex to hire and manage them or because they simply don’t think the talent is good enough. “There’s been a new wave of tremendous talent, a really high bar that is equal or even better than the U.S.,” she said of the global workforce. And that’s where MAVI comes in, which, Liu said, also helps companies handle the unglamorous work that comes with hiring global talent, like managing cross-border contracts, legal and compliance, and even payroll. She said the company focuses on quickly finding full-time, long-term placements that augment in-house finance teams, with a focus on mid-level and senior-level positions. Liu has worked at Ramp, Lyft, and Dropbox. She said working at these companies made her realize that more automation tools can’t fix all the problems in accounting. “AI will automate away many entry-level roles in finance and accounting, which will further exacerbate the talent shortage at the mid-level experience level, given there will be less entry-level talent growing into the mid-level over time,” Liu said. So no matter how many AI tools are released to automate grunt work, companies still need experienced humans to make judgment calls on critical work. In fact, she said, she’s noticed that the more AI tools a company adopts, the more pressure that adds to those in senior roles. “They are increasingly expected to add more of their reasoning skills,” she continued. “Finance teams are now being pushed to do more with less.” " Source: https://lnkd.in/enn-DUkQ

Back from Japan and thinking about the next version of how I work.

If you’re hiring freelance or contract help at the design/dev intersection, these are the problems I keep seeing at seed and Series A:

- UI is not consistent, team is shipping fast
- shadcn is installed, but not actually adopted, agents are shipping UI and not fully trusted
- PRs go out without a designer review, so the system drifts

That’s when the real work started. Guardrails, agent dos and don’ts, and how teams keep a design system alive when habits and AI are both pulling it apart.

📄 Ask most leadership teams if they have an AI governance program, and they'll say yes. Ask if they know every AI tool employees are actually using this week, and the room goes quiet.
That gap has a name: shadow AI.

Gartner's 2026 survey found 68% of employees use AI tools their IT team has zero visibility into. IBM's 2025 breach report found shadow AI adds $670,000 to the average breach cost and in 97% of those incidents, there were no AI access controls in place. You can't govern what you can't see, and most organizations aren't blind by accident. Nobody built the process to look.

Where it actually lives:
📋 The pasted prompt; a contract, a patient record, unreleased financials, dropped into a public chatbot to "just check something quick." No DPA, no idea where that data goes next.

🔌 The unapproved integration; an AI plugin connected to email or CRM because it saves twenty minutes. IT never sees the request, because there wasn't one.

📊 The unlogged decision; a hiring call, a risk score, quietly shaped by a tool that was never assessed, never inventoried, with no audit trail if anyone ever asks why.

None of this is malicious. It's people working around a gap official tooling left open  which is exactly why banning tools doesn't close it. It just pushes the same behavior further out of sight.

An ISO/IEC 42001-aligned AIMS treats this as a visibility problem before it's a policy one.  Risk assessment can't run on a tool nobody knows exists. Governance-by-design starts with an honest inventory, not a policy sitting next to a workforce that never stopped adopting.

Shadow AI isn't a compliance footnote. It's the governance program you think you have, minus everything you can't see.
💬 Block and accept people route around it, or build a sanctioned alternative fast enough that shadow AI has no reason to exist? Which have you actually seen work?

Ageism is not new.

Your parents hit it. 
Your grandparents hit it. 

But at least they had somewhere to land.

Defined benefit pensions. 
Retirement accounts that actually grew. 
A social contract that said if you worked hard for thirty years, you got to stop working. 
Florida. Golf. 
Sunday dinners where they did not check their phones because there was no phone to check.

We don't have that and may never again.

Most of us in tech over fifty are watching the same ageism play out, but without the exit ramp. 
The pension is gone. 
The 401k got hit in 2001, then 2008, then 2020. 

Social Security math does not work the way it used to. 
And the job market keeps writing descriptions for someone twenty-eight years old with fifteen years of AI experience and a willingness to work for less than we made in 2015.

So what do you do?

Some people are retiring to Portugal. Mexico. Southeast Asia. 
Places where a dollar stretches and the weather is decent, and nobody cares how old you are as long as you can pay rent. 

I know people doing this. Smart people. 
People who built enterprise infrastructures for Fortune 500 companies and decided the math in the US no longer worked.

I get it. Okay, I moved to Israel, not exactly the cheapest solution.

We built things that still run. 

We are the people who know where the bodies are buried and why the thing still works. 
Companies filter us out before a human sees the resume, and then they spend three years and twice the budget trying to replace what we know in our sleep.

You can't stop the clock. 
But you can stop pretending that filtering out experience is a feature of your hiring process. 

If you are over fifty in enterprise IT and the math is not adding up, you are not imagining it. 
And you are not alone.

Building a software product isn't just about paying the development bill and going live. The ongoing operational surprises are what usually break startup budgets.

Here are 3 technical concepts non-technical founders must clarify before signing a contract with any dev agency:

1. Caching
If your app queries the database for every single repeated action (like loading homepage products or user profiles), performance crawls and your cloud bill skyrockets. Proper caching stores frequent data in high-speed memory for instant access.
Ask them: "What is your caching strategy to keep response times fast and server costs low?"

2. Zero-Downtime Deployment
Deploying a bug fix or new feature shouldn't require taking your app offline. Zero-downtime deployment switches users smoothly to the new version without showing a "Site Under Maintenance" screen during peak business hours.
Ask them: "Will deployments interrupt active user sessions or require downtime?"

3. Third-Party APIs & Recurring Costs
Google Maps, SMS gateways (OTP), payment processors, and AI services are not included in your development fee. They charge usage-based monthly bills directly to your credit card.
Ask them: "What third-party services are required, and what is the estimated monthly recurring cost at 1,000 / 10,000 users?"

The T&T Partners team presents our latest assessment on AI hiring tools and discrimination liability.

A retail chain screens store-manager applications with an AI tool; because the tool scores graduation year, no applicant over 45 is invited to interview (fictional example). From 1 October 2026, under Connecticut law, using an automated employment-related decision technology will be no defence to a discrimination complaint; anti-bias testing may be weighed as evidence.

Turkish law points the same way. Law No. 6701 bans age discrimination in applications and selection criteria; before the Equality Institution, once the applicant shows strong indications, the employer must prove it did not discriminate, and an administrative fine may follow. An employee facing discriminatory promotion or dismissal may claim up to four months’ wages (Labour Law Art. 5). Under the Data Protection Law (KVKK) Art. 11, a result reached solely by automated analysis can be challenged, so genuine review by an authorised person matters.

Source: Connecticut Public Act 26-15, Secs. 7–14; notice duties apply from 1 October 2027 and the developer may assume them by contract. The Act does not bind in Türkiye; it reaches Turkish employers assessing staff or applicants in Connecticut and Turkish HR-tech vendors selling there.

Connecticut’ta 1 Ekim 2026’dan itibaren otomatik istihdam kararı teknolojisinin kullanılması ayrımcılık şikâyetinde savunma sayılmayacak; yanlılık testleri delil olarak değerlendirilebilecek.

Türk hukukunda da 6701 sayılı Kanun başvuru ve seçim kriterlerinde yaşa dayalı ayrımcılığı yasaklar; TİHEK’e başvuruda aday kuvvetli emare gösterirse ayrımcılık yapmadığını işveren ispat eder, ihlal hâlinde idarî para cezası gündeme gelebilir. Terfi veya fesihte ayrımcılığa uğrayan çalışan dört aya kadar ücret tutarında tazminat isteyebilir (İş K. m. 5). KVKK m. 11 münhasıran otomatik analizle ortaya çıkan aleyhe sonuca itiraz hakkı tanıdığından, yetkili bir kişinin çıktıyı gerçekten incelemesi önem taşır.

Kaynak: Connecticut Public Act 26-15, Sec. 7–14; bildirim yükümlülükleri 1 Ekim 2027’den itibaren uygulanır ve geliştirici bunları sözleşmeyle üstlenebilir. Düzenleme Türkiye’de bağlayıcı değil; Connecticut’taki çalışan veya adayları değerlendiren Türk işverenleri ve orada satış yapan Türk İK teknolojisi şirketlerini etkiler.

An employer list can look precise and still leave a rep guessing.

A company name, employee count, and address tell you almost nothing about why the account deserves attention. Useful employer intelligence brings together operational context, likely stakeholders, recent developments, relationship history, and a credible reason to begin a conversation.

AI can organize the first research pass. LinkedIn can reveal people and connections. Public sources may show hiring, expansion, contracts, leadership changes, or new facilities. CRM history can show whether your organization already knows more than it realizes.

Before anyone reaches out, the team should have provisional answers to three questions: Why does this employer belong on the list? Who is most likely to care? What makes the conversation relevant now?

Research creates a working hypothesis. Human judgment determines whether the evidence is credible and the opportunity deserves attention.
